title: Processes as variable embodiments
kind: primary journal article, version of record
locators: Publisher full text §§2, 3.1–3.2; A1–A12; V1′–V3′; footnotes 10–17. Web-accessed publisher page: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11229-024-04505-2
assumptions: The paper presents a descriptive ontology of processes as variable embodiments. In §§3.1–3.2 it distinguishes processes from events, uses temporalized functional constitution K, adopts classical mereology while rejecting manifestation-as-process-part V4*, relates event parts to temporary process parts by A9–A10, and matches local/global pro-tem properties by A11–A12. V1′–V3′ concern existence, temporal location, and identity via manifestation profiles. §4 calls unity/individuation principles crucial and develops a taxonomy beyond the fragment audited here.
conclusion: The displayed clauses constrain event/process manifestation structure but do not define a standpoint-relative concrete-inventory predicate or state the proposed occurrence-to-current-concreteness bridge. A11 is a property-correspondence schema; A12 matches global pro-tem property truth to manifestation truth. The paper states that processes accumulate temporal parts and that earlier parts can become inaccessible, but these claims alone do not settle the added C predicate.
proof_status: Formal axioms and postulates stated in philosophical ontology article; no formal proof system or machine-checked verification claimed. This review independently checks the proposed model against displayed formulas and source exposition, not the entire ontology.
open_questions: Whether the paper's broader unity/individuation taxonomy or a defensible substantive reading of concrete inventory supplies a bridge beyond the displayed fragment; whether CEM is intended globally across categories or relative to the typed mereologies used in the formulas.
relevance: Primary source audit for regular-open event/process countermodel and the scope of the occurrence-to-current-concreteness inference.
limits: Publisher HTML full text read. Audit is bounded to §§2–3.2, A1–A12, V1′–V3′, and footnotes 10–17; later taxonomy is consulted only to establish that unity and individuation are additional concerns, not reconstructed or audited.
